extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors preparing manuscripts (particularly Cranfield University researchers) who must write a data availability statement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing a Data Availability Statement (DAS) for research publications, covering required content, example phrasings for common scenarios, anti-patterns, and placement/linking best practices. Intended to ensure compliance with funder/university policies and journal expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a Data Availability Statement (DAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data availability statements, also known as data access statements, are included in publications to describe where the data associated with the paper is available, and under what conditions the data can be accessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are required by the university as part of the commitment to open research, by many funders, and research journals, as well as the UKRI Common Principles on Data Policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: include a DAS for publicly funded research (and always include a DAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research articles that result from public funding of research (including substantive positions) must include a data availability statement (DAS), even where there are no data associated with the article or the data are inaccessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cranfield’s Open Research Policy also states you must ensure published results always include a data availability statement (even if no new data has been produced). Read the full UKRI policy to ensure you know what your responsibilities are.

rubrics_metrics.name: State where the data can be accessed (repository preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your statement should typically include where the data can be accessed (preferably a data repository, like CORD in CERES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the NAME OF REPOSITORY (e.g., CORD) and a persistent identifier or URL so readers can find the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a persistent identifier (DOI/accession number/URL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a persistent identifier, such as a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) or accession number, or a link to a permanent record for the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague repository references without a persistent identifier. Examples show: '...available from (NAME OF REPOSITORY) at (DOI, ACCESSION NUMBER OR URL)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe any restrictions and justify them
rubrics_metrics.description: Include details of any restrictions on accessing the data and a justifiable explanation (e.g., for ethical, legal, or commercial reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If access is restricted, explain why and how access can be obtained (e.g., 'Access to the data is subject to approval and a data sharing agreement due to (GIVE REASONS WHY ACCESS TO THE DATA IS RESTRICTED)'). Under some circumstances (e.g., participants did not agree for their data to be shared) it may be appropriate to explain that the data are not available at all — in this case give clear and justified reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open data repository statement (sample phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to state that data are openly available in a repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “Data supporting this study are openly available from (NAME OF REPOSITORY, e.g., CORD) at (DOI, ACCESSION NUMBER OR URL)”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargoed data statement (sample phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to state that data are in a repository but subject to an embargo, including timeframe and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “Data supporting this study will be available from (NAME OF REPOSITORY, e.g., CORD) at (DOI, ACCESSION NUMBER OR URL) following a 6 month embargo” (and explain why).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted-access repository statement (sample phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to state that data are held in a repository but access is restricted for legal/ethical/commercial reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “Data supporting this study are available from (NAME OF REPOSITORY, e.g., CORD) at (DOI, ACCESSION NUMBER OR URL). Access to the data is subject to approval and a data sharing agreement due to (GIVE REASONS WHY ACCESS TO THE DATA IS RESTRICTED)”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party/licensed data (secondary analysis) statement
rubrics_metrics.description: How to describe use of third-party data that cannot be shared by the author because of licence restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “This study used third party data made available under licence that the author does not have permission to share. Requests to access the data should be directed to (THIRD PARTY) at (URL/CONTACT DETAILS)”.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data included as supplementary information
rubrics_metrics.description: How to state that supporting data are included within the article or supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “Data supporting this study are included within the article and/or supporting materials” (Raw data etc in CORD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data cannot be shared (explain why)
rubrics_metrics.description: When data cannot be shared due to ethical, legal, or commercial restrictions, explain that and give reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “Data supporting this study cannot be made available due to (GIVE REASONS WHY THE DATA CANNOT BE SHARED)”. Provide clear and justified reasons (e.g., participant consent issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: No new data generated or analysed (use explicit statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no new data have been created (for example in a review), include an explicit statement that data sharing is not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample: “No new data were created or analysed during this study. Data sharing is not applicable to this article.” Use this in situations such as a review, where no new data have been created.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ‘contact the author’ as the sole DAS
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple direction to contact the author may not be considered acceptable by some funders and publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider setting up a shared email address for your research group or use an existing departmental address. Do not rely solely on 'Data available on request' for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of poor and insufficient DAS (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that are likely to be considered inadequate or unacceptable as DAS content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed as poor: • “Data available on request / reasonable request” (directs reader to contact author) • “Data are available in a public, open access repository.” (vague, no persistent identifier) • Placing the data access statement only in the Methods section instead of a DAS section • “Not applicable” or unclear statement on whether there is data. These are insufficient for many funders/publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of the DAS in the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Where to include the data availability statement in your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a journal provides a “data availability” or “data access” section, use it. If no such section exists, you can place your statement in the acknowledgements section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link datasets to your article after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the dataset and article are reciprocally connected by updating repository records after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once your article is published, update your repository project with the DOI for your article (you will receive this upon publication). Linking supporting data to your publication ensures your data and paper are connected and that you receive credit.
